chunks: And a group informed me, from Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn Ali ibn al-Husayn ibn Musa ibn Babawayh, who said: Muhammad ibn Ibrahim ibn Ishaq al-Talqani informed me, saying:

I was with Shaykh Abul-Qasim ibn Ruh (may Allah be pleased with him) in the company of a group, among them Ali ibn Isa al-Qasri. A man stood up to him and said: 'I wish to ask you about something.' He replied to him: 'Ask whatever occurs to you.' He asked questions, which we have mentioned in other places.

Muhammad ibn Ibrahim ibn Ishaq said: So I returned to Shaykh Abul-Qasim ibn Ruh (may Allah be pleased with him) the next day, while I was saying to myself: 'Do you think he mentioned to us yesterday from his own self (opinion)?'

He initiated us and said: 'O Muhammad ibn Ibrahim! That the sky should tear open and birds snatch me, or the wind carry me down from a distant place, is more beloved to me than that I should say in the religion of Allah, Exalted and Mighty, according to my own opinion and from my own self. Rather, that is from the Source, and heard from the Proof (Imam), peace be upon him.'
ai.seo_question: What is the source of Shaykh al-Ruh's religious knowledge according to this hadith?
ai.summary: This narrative from Kitab al-Ghayba highlights the concept of *al-rawi* (the transmitter) in Shia theology, where Shaykh al-Ruh serves as a reliable conduit for the Imam's teachings rather than an independent jurist relying on personal reasoning (*ra'y*). His declaration underscores the authority of the Hidden Imam as the ultimate source of religious knowledge, reinforcing the scholarly tradition that transmitted hadith are divinely sanctioned rather than merely human interpretations.
